label: L5
title: Supervised Learning: One Generic Algorithm
brief: Lecture 5 moves from calling pre-trained LLMs to training models from the loss function up with one common recipe. Every supervised learning problem has two ingredients: a function class indexed by parameters θ, and a loss that scores a single prediction. The task is to find a θ that makes the average loss small. Squared error suits real-valued targets. Binary cross-entropy suits probabilities because confidently wrong predictions are unboundedly bad (predicting 0.001 for a true 1 costs 6.91, while squared error caps at 1), and K-class cross-entropy with a one-hot target keeps only the true class's term. Gradient descent (step opposite the gradient, scaled by a step size η) is the one generic optimizer, and with autograd (loss.backward()) the same few lines of torch fit linear regression, a 7,850-parameter softmax classifier and a 203,530-parameter one-hidden-layer network; only the function class changes. The lecture closes with two practical fixes: capacity lets a model memorise, so a held-out validation set decides when to stop, and full-batch gradients are too expensive, so stochastic gradient descent averages over mini-batches (469 updates per epoch at batch size 128 on 60,000 examples).
kp: Supervised learning in one line: given a function class $f_\theta$ and a per-prediction loss, find a θ that makes the average loss small.
A loss takes two numbers (prediction, truth) and returns one. It knows nothing about parameters, features or data sets, and must be smooth enough to differentiate.
Squared error for regression: zero when right, penalises both directions equally, differentiable everywhere unlike $|\hat y - y|$; its derivative is the mistake doubled.
Binary cross-entropy $-[y\log\hat y + (1-y)\log(1-\hat y)]$: confidently wrong is unboundedly bad ($-\ln 0.001 = 6.91$), while squared error caps the penalty at 1.
K-class cross-entropy with a one-hot target reduces to $-\log\hat y_c$ for the true class c; its derivative is large when $\hat y_c$ is small.
Gradient descent: $\theta \leftarrow \theta - \eta\nabla L(\theta)$. Too small η crawls, too large overshoots and oscillates, larger still diverges; the boundary depends on the problem.
Linear-regression gradient: grad = (2/N)·Xᵀ(Xa − y), with X N×d, residuals N×1, gradient d×1. Autograd (loss.backward()) replaces this hand derivation for good.
Torch loop: model (function class), loss, opt.zero_grad() (gradients accumulate), loss.backward() (∂L/∂θ into θ.grad), opt.step(). Only the model line changes for softmax, a network or a Transformer.
Clothing-image test accuracy: linear softmax 0.839 → one 256-unit ReLU hidden layer 0.875 → same network with Adam 0.888.
Train fits weights, validation decides when to stop and picks hyperparameters, test is touched once. SGD uses mini-batches: noisy but right on average and far cheaper per step.

topics.x: Given N labelled examples (x, y), we want a function that maps x to a good approximation of y and still works on examples never seen. The two ingredients, a function class indexed by θ and a loss, combine into the average loss. Supervised learning means finding θ that makes it small with one generic optimiser, because a neural network has no lm/glm-style special solver.

Squared error for a number, binary cross-entropy for the probability of a 0/1 outcome, and K-class cross-entropy for K probabilities with a one-hot target. Cross-entropy penalises confident wrong answers without bound, and its derivative blows up as the prediction approaches the wrong extreme, giving large corrective gradients.

Compute the slope where you stand and move opposite its sign: w ← w − η g′(w), with big steps where it is steep and small steps where it is flat. With many parameters the gradient ∇L holds one partial derivative per parameter. The step size η is a hyperparameter chosen before training, alongside hidden size and training length; the data are given and the parameters are learned.

topics.n: Linear regression by gradient descent and autograd
topics.x: The loop is yhat = X@a, resid = yhat − y, loss = mean(resid²), grad = (2/N)Xᵀresid, a ← a − η·grad. Torch replaces each line: nn.Linear holds θ, F.mse_loss computes the loss, loss.backward() fills θ.grad by multiplying local derivatives backwards (automatic differentiation), and opt.step() applies the update. All three versions give θ = (1.993, −2.999) with loss 0.0932.

topics.n: Softmax classifier and a neural network
topics.x: For 784-pixel images and 10 classes, nn.Linear(784, 10) produces ten scores (7,850 parameters) that feed softmax and cross-entropy, with mini-batches from a DataLoader. Inserting nn.Linear(784, 256) + nn.ReLU() before nn.Linear(256, 10) gives 203,530 parameters and changes nothing else in the loop; test accuracy rises from 0.839 to 0.875, and to 0.888 with Adam.

Training error falls whether the model is too simple or memorising, so it cannot tell you which you have. Hold data back and stop when the validation loss turns upward. In the notebook, with far too much model for 60 examples, training loss falls to 0.0008 while validation loss bottoms at 0.96 at step 200 and climbs to 1.149.

Each full gradient step sums over every training point, so one step costs one pass over the data. SGD averages the gradient over a small random mini-batch: noisier, but right on average and hundreds of times cheaper. On 60,000 examples, batch 128 gives 469 updates per epoch; full-batch descent needed 122 epochs (7.32 million examples processed) to reach the loss mini-batches reached in one.

cards.f: The two ingredients of every supervised learning problem?
cards.b: A function class (a family of predictors indexed by parameters θ) and a loss (how bad a single prediction is). Together they give the average loss; supervised learning means finding θ that makes it small.
cards.x: The generic optimiser is the third piece, and it is the same for every problem.

cards.f: What goes into a loss function, and what does it know about?
cards.b: Two numbers, a prediction and the truth, and it returns one number. It knows nothing about parameters, features or data sets.
cards.x: Small when close, large when far, smooth enough to differentiate.

cards.f: Why squared error rather than |ŷ − y| for regression?
cards.b: Both are zero when right and penalise both directions equally, but squared error is differentiable everywhere; its derivative 2(ŷ − y) is the size of the mistake, doubled.
cards.x: Absolute error has a kink at zero.

cards.f: True y = 1, prediction ŷ = 0.01: log loss vs squared error?
cards.x: Squared error caps the penalty at 1; cross-entropy is unbounded.

cards.f: Binary cross-entropy: formula, and what survives when y = 1 and when y = 0?
cards.b: $-[y\log\hat y + (1-y)\log(1-\hat y)]$. y = 1 leaves $-\log\hat y$; y = 0 leaves $-\log(1-\hat y)$.
cards.x: One of the two terms always vanishes.

cards.f: Why does BCE give enormous gradients for confidently wrong predictions?
cards.b: The derivative has ŷ (or 1 − ŷ) in the denominator, e.g. $\frac{d}{d\hat y}(-\log\hat y) = -1/\hat y$, which explodes as ŷ nears the wrong extreme.

cards.f: K-class cross-entropy with a one-hot target?
cards.b: Only the true class's term survives: loss = $-\log\hat y_c$. Its derivative is large when the predicted probability of the true class is small.
cards.x: Number → squared error; two classes → BCE; K classes → cross-entropy.

cards.f: Gradient descent update for one variable?
cards.b: $w \leftarrow w - \eta\,g'(w)$. A positive slope moves w down and a negative slope moves it up; steep ground gives big steps, flat ground small ones.
cards.x: It needs no knowledge of where, or whether, a minimum exists.

cards.f: What happens as the step size η grows?
cards.b: Too small: crawls. About right: converges. Too large: overshoots, then oscillates. Larger still: diverges. The divergence boundary is a property of the problem (η = 2/9 for the notes' example).
cards.x: η is the crucial knob in gradient descent.

cards.f: Three kinds of quantities in training?
cards.b: Given: data x, y (measured, never changed). Learned: the parameters inside f (set by gradient descent). Chosen by you: hyperparameters, i.e. η, hidden size, how long to train.
cards.x: Hyperparameters are fixed before training starts.

cards.f: Matrix-form MSE gradient for linear regression, with shapes?
cards.b: grad = (2/N)·Xᵀ(Xa − y). X is N×d, the residuals N×1, the gradient d×1 (one number per parameter).
cards.x: Derived by hand once (§4.1 of the notes), never again.

cards.f: What do opt.zero_grad(), loss.backward() and opt.step() do?
cards.b: zero_grad clears old gradients, since they accumulate. backward walks the graph backwards so every ∂L/∂θ lands in θ.grad. step applies θ ← θ − η·grad.
cards.x: Forget zero_grad and old gradients get added to new ones.

cards.f: How many parameters does nn.Linear(784, 10) have?
cards.x: Each class score has its own row of 784 weights.
Only the function class changed, by two inserted lines of code.

cards.f: The jobs of the train, validation and test sets?
cards.b: Train: fit the weights (the only set gradient descent sees). Validation: decide when to stop, and choose hidden size and step size. Test: touch once, at the end.
cards.x: Every look at the test set makes it a little less honest.

cards.f: Updates per epoch on 60,000 examples: full-batch GD vs SGD with batch 128?
cards.b: GD: 1 update per epoch using all the data. SGD: 469 updates (60,000/128 ≈ 468.75, so 469 batches), each on 128 points. Noisier, but right on average.
cards.x: Full batch needed 122 epochs to reach the loss SGD reached in one.

quiz.q: In the lecture's one-line statement, supervised learning is to…
o: Find a θ that makes the average loss small
Find the function class with the most parameters
Find a loss that is zero on the training data
Find the subset of data that minimises the loss
quiz.e: 'Supervised Learning: Find a θ that makes the average loss small.' The function class and loss are fixed ingredients; the data are given and never changed.

quiz.q: Which loss pairs with predicting K class probabilities?
quiz.e: The three-losses slide pairs a number with squared error, one probability (two classes) with binary cross-entropy, and K probabilities with cross-entropy. BCE alone covers only the two-class case.

quiz.q: True label y = 1; the model predicts ŷ = 0.10. What are the log loss and the squared error?
True label y = 0; the model predicts ŷ = 0.999. Which is correct?
o: Cross-entropy is −ln(0.001) ≈ 6.91, while squared error is ≈ 1.00
Cross-entropy is ≈ 0.001 because ŷ is close to 1
quiz.e: For y = 0 the surviving term is −ln(1 − ŷ) = −ln 0.001 ≈ 6.91, while (0.999 − 0)² ≈ 1.00. Squared error caps at 1; cross-entropy does not.

quiz.q: With y = 1 and ŷ = 0.001, compare the derivative with respect to ŷ of binary cross-entropy and of squared error.
o: BCE is not differentiable at ŷ = 0.001
quiz.e: For y = 1, BCE = −log ŷ with derivative −1/ŷ = −1000; the denominator going to zero is what makes confident mistakes produce enormous gradients. 6.91 and 1 are the loss values, not their derivatives.

quiz.q: Why does the lecture prefer squared error to |ŷ − y| for regression?
o: It penalises over-predictions more than under-predictions
It is zero only when the prediction is wrong
quiz.e: Both are zero when right and symmetric, but |ŷ − y| has a kink at zero; squared error is differentiable everywhere. The 'capped at 1' property applies only to squared error on probabilities.

quiz.q: With a one-hot target over K classes, the cross-entropy for one example equals…
o: −log of the predicted probability of the true class
The sum of −log ŷ_k over all K classes
The squared distance between ŷ and the one-hot vector
quiz.e: Every y_k is zero except the true class, so only that term survives. Using the largest predicted probability is wrong when the model's top class is not the true class.

quiz.q: At the current point the derivative is g′(w) = −3. Gradient descent moves w…
o: Nowhere, because the slope is negative
quiz.e: Move opposite the sign of the derivative: w − η(−3) = w + 3η, so w increases. GD never knows where the minimum is; it only follows the local slope.

quiz.q: g(w) = (w − 3)², current w = 5, step size η = 0.1. What is the next iterate?
quiz.e: g′(5) = 2(5 − 3) = 4, so w ← 5 − 0.1 × 4 = 4.6. Adding the step gives 5.4 (wrong sign); dropping the factor 2 gives 4.8.

quiz.q: Same g(w) = (w − 3)², start at w = 5, but now η = 1.0. What does gradient descent do?
quiz.e: w − 3 is multiplied by (1 − 2η) each step. With η = 1 that factor is −1, so 5 → 1 → 5 → …. One-step convergence happens at η = 0.5, divergence needs η > 1, and crawling needs a tiny η. This is the 'overshoots, then oscillates' regime at the edge of divergence.

quiz.q: Which of these is a hyperparameter rather than a learned parameter?
o: A bias of the output layer
The label y of an example
quiz.e: Hyperparameters (η, hidden size, how long to train) are chosen before training. Weights and biases are learned by gradient descent; labels are given data.

quiz.q: X is N×d. In grad = (2/N)·Xᵀ(Xa − y), what are the shapes of (Xa − y) and of grad?
quiz.e: Xa − y has one residual per example (N×1); Xᵀ (d×N) times that gives one number per parameter (d×1). Swapping them confuses examples with parameters.

quiz.q: A student deletes opt.zero_grad() from the torch training loop. What goes wrong?
o: Gradients accumulate across steps, so each update uses the sum of current and past gradients
loss.backward() raises an error on the second step
The parameters are reset to zero every step
Nothing, because opt.step() clears the gradients itself
quiz.e: The slide notes 'gradients accumulate — clear them'. backward adds into θ.grad rather than overwriting it, so stale gradients pile up silently without any error.

o: Computes every ∂L/∂θ by walking the graph backwards (multiplying local derivatives) and stores it in θ.grad
Applies the update θ ← θ − η∇L
Computes the loss on the validation set
quiz.e: backward is automatic differentiation: it fills θ.grad. Applying the update is opt.step(), the tempting confusion.

quiz.q: How many parameters does nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(784, 256), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(256, 10)) have?
quiz.e: (784×256 + 256) + (256×10 + 10) = 200,960 + 2,570 = 203,530. 203,264 omits the 266 biases, 200,960 counts only the first layer, and 7,850 is the linear softmax model.

quiz.q: Going from the linear softmax classifier to the one-hidden-layer network, which parts of the training program change?
o: The loss switches from cross-entropy to squared error
The gradient must now be derived by hand
The optimiser must switch to Adam for a network to train
quiz.e: Function class changed; loss and loss.backward() unchanged. SGD trained the network to 0.875; Adam was an optional one-word change that raised accuracy to 0.888.

quiz.q: Training loss falls to 0.0008 while validation loss bottoms at 0.96 at step 200 and then climbs to 1.149. What should you do?
o: Stop at about step 200, chosen by the validation loss
Train longer, since the training loss is still falling
Choose the stopping step by looking at the test loss
Stop only when the training loss reaches exactly zero
quiz.e: Validation decides when to stop; the training loss is not what you care about, and it falls whether or not the model memorises. Choosing the step on test data spends the test set's honesty.

quiz.q: 60,000 training examples, mini-batch size 128. How many SGD updates happen in 3 epochs?
quiz.e: 60,000/128 = 468.75, so 469 batches and 469 updates per epoch; 3 × 469 = 1,407. Three updates is full-batch GD; 180,000 counts examples processed, not updates; 469 is one epoch.

written.q: Explain why a classifier that outputs probabilities is trained with cross-entropy rather than squared error. Give the binary cross-entropy formula, a numerical comparison, and the consequence for gradient descent. Then state what changes for K classes.
written.m: BCE = $-[y\log\hat y + (1-y)\log(1-\hat y)]$; for y = 1 only $-\log\hat y$ survives, for y = 0 only $-\log(1-\hat y)$. A confidently wrong prediction should be punished heavily. With y = 1: ŷ = 0.5 costs 0.69 (BCE) vs 0.25 (squared error); ŷ = 0.01 costs 4.61 vs 0.98; ŷ = 0.001 costs 6.91 vs 1.00. Squared error caps the penalty at 1, while cross-entropy is unbounded. For gradient descent, the BCE derivative has ŷ (or 1 − ŷ) in the denominator (e.g. −1/ŷ), so it is enormous for confident mistakes (−1000 at ŷ = 0.001 vs about −2 for squared error), and the update corrects them strongly. With K classes and a one-hot target, cross-entropy reduces to $-\log\hat y_c$ for the true class c, which is large, with a large derivative, when the model gives the true class a small probability.
k: Correct BCE formula and the surviving term for each label
Numerical comparison from the table, e.g. 4.61 vs 0.98 at ŷ = 0.01
Squared error is bounded by 1 on probabilities; cross-entropy is unbounded
Gradient argument: denominator → 0 gives large corrective steps
K-class case: one-hot target leaves −log ŷ_c

written.q: Starting from the torch training loop for linear regression, describe exactly what changes to (a) train a 10-class softmax classifier on 784-pixel images and (b) add one 256-unit ReLU hidden layer. Give each model's parameter count. Then explain (c) why you would train on mini-batches and (d) how you decide when to stop.
written.m: Linear regression loop: model = nn.Linear(d, 1); opt = optim.SGD(model.parameters(), lr=η); for each step: loss = F.mse_loss(model(X).squeeze(), y); opt.zero_grad(); loss.backward(); opt.step(). (a) The function class becomes nn.Linear(784, 10), giving ten scores turned into probabilities by softmax, with 784×10 + 10 = 7,850 parameters. The loss becomes cross_entropy. Data come through DataLoader(data, batch_size=128) with an epoch loop. zero_grad/backward/step are unchanged and no derivative is worked out by hand (test accuracy 0.839). (b) Only the model changes: nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(784, 256), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(256, 10)), with (784×256 + 256) + (256×10 + 10) = 203,530 parameters; loss, optimiser and loop are untouched (accuracy 0.875, 0.888 with Adam). (c) A full gradient sums over every training example, so each step is a whole pass over the data. A mini-batch gradient is noisy but right on average and far cheaper: 469 updates per epoch at batch 128 on 60,000 examples, against 1 for full batch, which needed 122 epochs to reach the loss mini-batches reached in one. (d) More capacity lets the model memorise, and the training loss falls either way, so hold out a validation set and stop when its loss turns upward (e.g. minimum at step 200 in the notebook). Validation also picks hidden size and η; the test set is used once, at the end.
k: States that only the model line changes for (b), and the model + loss + loader for (a)
Role of zero_grad/backward/step unchanged; autograd removes hand derivatives
Mini-batch argument: cost per step vs noise; 469 updates/epoch
Early stopping on validation loss; test touched once
